fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces modulation-period-controlled interface coherency with stress-induced short-range ordering as the governing variable, without evidence that such ordering occurs at these multilayer interfaces.
It proposes moderately elevated-temperature creep, whereas the target behavior was established under room-temperature nanoindentation.
It omits the decisive comparison among coherent, semicoherent, and grain-boundary-dominated multilayers produced by varying layer thickness.
It does not predict the distinctive maximum creep resistance and minimum stress exponent of the 16 nm semicoherent multilayer.
The cited evidence concerns generic HEA properties and strain-induced rearrangement or clustering, not sustained-load interfacial ordering governing creep in FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayers.
explanation: The response addresses progressive deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers and offers a falsifiable SRO-based experiment, so it has some broad problem alignment and experimental discriminability. Scientifically, however, it does not reconstruct the target. The relevant intervention is variation of the modulation period to select coherent, semicoherent, or grain-boundary-dominated structures, followed by room-temperature nanoindentation creep. The proposed elevated-temperature SRO transition neither matches the semicoherent-interface/dislocation-pileup/interfacial-amorphization mechanism nor explains the observed low stress exponent and superior creep resistance at 16 nm. Its baseline is only an unloaded initial state rather than the required layer-thickness controls. E2 gives limited support for strain-induced atomic rearrangement in a related alloy, but does not validate a clustering-to-ordering transition at multilayer interfaces or establish that it controls creep; E1 is only generic background. The hypothesis is novel but insufficiently evidenced and materially inconsistent with the reported conditions and outcomes.
